questions.q: What is a "local hidden variable" model, in plain terms?
options: A quantum circuit that hides qubits from measurement
A classical model where correlation between two particles is explained by shared information fixed in advance and carried along with each particle, requiring no communication at measurement time
A variable that can only be observed by a local observer standing next to the apparatus
A type of error-correction code used in quantum hardware
questions.explain: A local hidden variable model explains correlation the same way two coins printed from the same secret script would: the agreement was baked in beforehand, and nothing needs to travel between the particles at measurement time.

questions.q: If you only ever measure a Bell pair in ONE fixed basis (the computational basis), can a local hidden-variable model reproduce the observed correlation exactly?
options: No — single-basis correlation already proves entanglement is not classical
Yes — a shared classical script reproduces the single-basis statistics (P(00)=P(11)=0.5, P(01)=P(10)=0) exactly, with no need to invoke anything quantum
No, because classical coins can never be correlated
Yes, but only if the coins are allowed to communicate during measurement
questions.explain: This lesson's key point is that single-basis correlation alone is NOT enough to rule out a classical explanation — a fixed shared script matches those numbers perfectly. The real test requires comparing multiple measurement bases, which is lesson 19's job.

questions.q: Why does a local hidden-variable script eventually fail to explain entangled correlations, according to this lesson?
options: Because classical scripts can never be normalized

Because the script has to commit in advance to an answer for every possible future measurement basis, and no such fixed script can reproduce the correlations quantum mechanics predicts across multiple different measurement angles
Because classical randomness is always biased
Because hidden variables are illegal to use in physics
questions.explain: The failure shows up specifically when measurements are taken at multiple different angles. A pre-committed script has to answer for every angle in advance, and no such script can reproduce the full multi-angle quantum correlation pattern — which is exactly what the CHSH inequality in lesson 19 quantifies.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what distinguishes genuine entanglement from shared classical randomness is specifically:
options: The single-basis correlation numbers, which look stronger for entangled qubits
The fact that entangled qubits are physically touching
The pattern of correlations measured ACROSS multiple different measurement bases, which exceeds what any local hidden-variable model can produce
The speed at which the two qubits were separated
questions.explain: The single-basis numbers are identical between the two models — that's exactly why this lesson emphasizes they don't settle the question. The real distinguishing signature only appears once multiple measurement settings are compared.

questions.q: Why does this distinction (multi-basis correlation beyond any classical model) matter for cryptography, as previewed in this lesson?
options: It doesn't — cryptography only cares about single-basis measurements

Because a protocol can use the violation of the classical correlation bound itself as proof that a real entangled pair (not a classical fake) is being used — the basis of device-independent quantum key distribution
Because classical randomness is always more secure than quantum randomness
Because entangled qubits cannot be intercepted by an eavesdropper under any circumstances
questions.explain: If entanglement were just shared classical randomness, it would offer nothing cryptographically new. Because multi-basis correlations provably exceed the classical bound, exceeding that bound in a protocol becomes verifiable evidence that genuine entanglement (not a classical substitute) is in use — the core idea behind device-independent QKD, detailed further in lesson 19.
